sections.heading: 2.2. Sinkhorn-Regularized Optimal Transport
sections.text: Optimal transport (OT) defines a principled measure of discrepancy between two discrete distributions over feature vectors. Let { u i } i = 1 m \{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} and { v j } j = 1 n \{v_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n} denote two sets of vectors, associated with probability weights a ∈ Δ m a\in\Delta^{m} and b ∈ Δ n b\in\Delta^{n} , respectively. Given a ground cost function c ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) c(\cdot,\cdot) , the cost matrix C ∈ ℝ + m × n C\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m\times n} is defined by C i ​ j = c ⁡ ( u i , v j ) C_{ij}=c(u_{i},v_{j}) . A transport plan Π ∈ ℝ + m × n \Pi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m\times n} quantifies the probability mass transported from u i u_{i} to v j v_{j} . The feasible set of couplings between a a and b b is given by: (2) 𝒰 ( a , b ) = { Π ∈ ℝ + m × n : Π 𝟏 = a , Π ⊤ 𝟏 = b } . \mathcal{U}(a,b)=\Bigl\{\Pi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m\times n}:\ \Pi\mathbf{1}=a,\ \Pi^{\top}\mathbf{1}=b\Bigr\}. The unregularized OT distance is then defined as: (3) OT ⁡ ( a , b , C ) = min Π ∈ 𝒰 ⁡ ( a , b ) ⁡ ⟨ Π , C ⟩ , ⟨ Π , C ⟩ = ∑ i , j Π i ​ j ​ C i ​ j , \mathrm{OT}(a,b;C)=\min_{\Pi\in\mathcal{U}(a,b)}\ \langle\Pi,C\rangle,\qquad\langle\Pi,C\rangle=\sum_{i,j}\Pi_{ij}C_{ij}, which measures the minimum expected transport cost ( Gabriel and Marco, 2019 ) . To obtain a smoother objective that can be computed efficiently, entropic regularization leads to the Sinkhorn-regularized OT value ( Cuturi, 2013 ) : (4) OT ε ​ ( a , b , C ) = min Π ∈ 𝒰 ⁡ ( a , b ) ⁡ ⟨ Π , C ⟩ − ε ​ ∑ i , j Π i ​ j ​ ( log ⁡ Π i ​ j − 1 ) , \mathrm{OT}_{\varepsilon}(a,b;C)=\min_{\Pi\in\mathcal{U}(a,b)}\ \langle\Pi,C\rangle-\varepsilon\sum_{i,j}\Pi_{ij}\big(\log\Pi_{ij}-1\big), where ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 controls the regularization strength. In practice, the value OT ε ​ ( a , b , C ) \mathrm{OT}_{\varepsilon}(a,b;C) is computed via Sinkhorn iterations; implementation details are provided in Appendix A.5 . Figure 2 . Overview of the SPOT framework. Stage I trains the student on SpanDrop sequences by anchoring <pause> hidden states to the corresponding teacher span under the frozen LM head, using a Sinkhorn-based alignment loss. Stage II applies RFT by selecting correct completions and preferring shorter ones, improving stability under external <pause> insertion.

sections.heading: 3.2. Training Data
sections.text: Given an input query x x , the teacher generates an explicit CoT sequence y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) . Consistent with the definition in Section 2 , we partition y y into M M consecutive reasoning spans { S i } i = 1 M \{S_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} , such that y = S 1 ​ ‖ ⋯ ‖ ​ S M y=S_{1}\|\cdots\|S_{M} . To construct SpanDrop instances, we sample a subset of span indices 𝒟 ⊆ { 1 , … , M } \mathcal{D}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\} by independently selecting each span with a probability of 0.3 0.3 . For each index i ∈ 𝒟 i\in\mathcal{D} , the corresponding span S i S_{i} is replaced by a single special token <pause> , resulting in the compressed sequence y ~ \tilde{y} . This substitution preserves the relative order of the remaining segments. The <pause> token is integrated into the tokenizer vocabulary and shares the embedding matrix E E with standard tokens. Consequently, each training instance constitutes a tuple ( x , y , y ~ ) (x,y,\tilde{y}) , comprising the input, the complete teacher trace, and the span-compressed sequence. During training, the teacher model processes the full sequence y y to yield the final-layer hidden states H tea = ( h 1 tea , … , h T tea ) H^{\text{tea}}=(h^{\text{tea}}_{1},\ldots,h^{\text{tea}}_{T}) . For a specific span S i S_{i} , we aggregate the corresponding teacher states into: (5) H tea ​ ( S i ) = [ h t tea ] y t ∈ S i ∈ ℝ | S i | × d , H^{\text{tea}}(S_{i})\;=\;\big[\,h^{\text{tea}}_{t}\,\big]_{y_{t}\in S_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|S_{i}|\times d}, which provides a variable-length representation of the span. Simultaneously, the student model processes the span-dropped sequence y ~ \tilde{y} , conditioned on x x . For each replaced span S i S_{i} ( i ∈ 𝒟 i\in\mathcal{D} ), let z i ∈ ℝ d z_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the student’s final-layer hidden state at the corresponding <pause> position. The training process aligns the single latent state z i z_{i} with the sequence of teacher states H tea ​ ( S i ) H^{\text{tea}}(S_{i}) derived from the omitted span, establishing the supervision target for the alignment objective detailed in Section 3.3 . To ensure computational efficiency, we impose a maximum limit on the number of teacher states per span, employing uniform subsampling when | S i | |S_{i}| exceeds this threshold (see Section 4.1 ).

sections.heading: A.7. LLM Judge Details
sections.text: To assess the faithfulness of compressed reasoning produced under inference-time external <pause> insertion, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge protocol. The judge is instructed to focus on (i) local transition coherence across the <pause> boundary and (ii) whether NEXT_SPAN relies on an intermediate conclusion not stated in the PREVIOUS_SPAN (i.e., evidence of meaningful compression), while strictly avoiding solving the problem or hallucinating missing steps. Box A.7 shows the full prompt used in our evaluation. LLM-as-a-Judge prompt used in our evaluation. <System Prompt> You are an evaluator of compressed reasoning quality around externally inserted <pause> markers. Your role is to assess local continuity and pause utilization only. Do not solve the problem. Do not rewrite the reasoning. Do not assume hidden steps beyond the provided text. Return only a valid JSON object. <User Prompt> You will evaluate one compressed reasoning instance. Scoring rubric (1--5): 1) local_continuity 5: NEXT_SPAN follows smoothly from PREVIOUS_SPAN; variable tracking is consistent; no contradictions. 4: Minor gap, but the intended bridge is clear and recoverable from the provided text. 3: Noticeable gap; at least one important bridge is ambiguous. 2: Major gap; NEXT_SPAN does not follow without substantial missing reasoning. 1: Contradictory, incoherent, or non-sequitur transition. 2) pause_utilization 5: Clear evidence that NEXT_SPAN uses an intermediate conclusion not explicitly stated in PREVIOUS_SPAN (a meaningful ‘‘jump’’ across <pause>). 4: Some evidence of an unstated intermediate conclusion; the jump is plausible from context. 3: Weak/ambiguous evidence; NEXT_SPAN could be derived without relying on an unstated intermediate result. 2: Little evidence of a jump; NEXT_SPAN is mostly a straightforward continuation or minor rewrite. 1: No evidence of utilization; <pause> appears unnecessary (e.g., repetition, filler, or restating the same point). Constraints: - Judge strictly from provided text. - Do not credit unobserved ‘‘implicit’’ steps unless trivially inferable. - Penalize restart/repetition/filler behavior when it harms coherence. - Keep rationale concise and specific. Return ONLY JSON with exactly this schema: { "local_continuity": 1, "pause_utilization": 1, "rationale": "", "missing_step": "", "error_type": "none", "confidence": 0.0 } Where: - rationale: short explanation for assigned scores ( ≤ \leq 80 words). - missing_step: brief missing bridge if any, else "". - error_type: one of ["none", "minor_gap", "major_gap", "contradiction", "restart", "repetition", "irrelevant", "format_issue", "insufficient_context"]. - confidence: real number in [0,1]. [PROBLEM] {question} [COMPRESSED_TRACE] {compressed_trace} [PREVIOUS_SPAN] {step_before} [NEXT_SPAN] {step_after} [FINAL_ANSWER] {final_answer}
